Back in 2008, at NVIDIA’s NVISION conference, MythBusters hosts Adam Savage and Jamie Hyneman built a rig to visualize the difference between a CPU and a GPU.

A CPU handles one task at a time, but does it fast and flexibly. That’s the single robotic arm, firing one paintball after another, building the image pixel by pixel.

A GPU trades flexibility for scale. Instead of doing one thing quickly, it does thousands of simple things at once. That’s the 1,100-barrel rig: every paintball fires simultaneously, so instead of one dot at a time, the entire Mona Lisa appears in about 80 milliseconds.

Neither is “better” outright. A CPU can still run complex, varied instructions in order, which is why your computer needs one no matter what. A GPU is only fast here because painting fixed dots of color breaks into thousands of identical, independent tasks with no dependency on each other.

That’s also why GPUs ended up powering AI. Training and running models means doing the same math operation across huge amounts of data simultaneously, the same parallel problem as the paintballs, just applied to neural networks instead of paint.

Did this demo actually make parallel computing click, or does it still feel like a fun visual without a real explanation?
